habit_line: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome, Remainder Riddlers! When we share things out, there are often some left over. Today the leftovers are clues: they tell us how many buses to book, which number is hiding, and how many tables are in the room.
do: Focus habit: Try - Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: “Pick one example and test it. What happens?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: I will call out some sweets and a group size. Show me the number of groups on one hand and the leftover on the other.
23 sweets in groups of 4. How many groups? How many left over? Which times-table fact helped you?
We will put 25 counters into groups of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Which group size do you think leaves nothing over? Write a guess.
stuck: Stuck: make the groups with counters and push the leftovers to one side.
Use a times-table fact: 6 × 4 = 24, so 25 in groups of 4 is 6 groups and 1 left over.
Ready for more: the Go further what-if on the slide: try 49 counters. Which group sizes leave 1 over? Why?

say: “38 sweets for 5 children. I count in 5s: 5 × 7 = 35, 5 × 8 = 40, too many. So each child gets 7.”
“I used 35, so 38 − 35 = 3 are left over. Is 3 smaller than 5? Yes. So 38 ÷ 5 = 7 r 3. Check: 7 × 5 + 3 = 38.”
“50 people, vans of 8: 50 ÷ 8 = 6 r 2. Those 2 people still need a ride, so 7 vans. But 50 cakes in boxes of 8 fill only 6 boxes. Same division, different answer, so I read the question again.”

do: Ask: “Is your remainder smaller than the number you divided by?”
Ask: “What happens to the leftover in this story?”
Ask: “How do you know there are no more numbers in your list?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Which times table do you need? Count up in it.”
Hint 2: “Groups × size + leftover gives the starting number.”
Hint 3: “List the numbers that fit one clue. Then test each one with the other clue.”

say: “Why can the remainder never be as big as the number we divide by?”
“75 ÷ 9 = 8 r 3. Why was the minibus answer 9, not 8?”
ask: “Why can the remainder never be as big as the number we divide by?”
If the leftover were as big as the group size, we could make one more group, so the remainder is always smaller. The 3 pupils left over still need a seat, so we need one more minibus: 9.

say: “Today you read the leftovers like clues. Inquirers ask what an answer means, not just what it is.”

p3l5-title.note: Objective: Divide with remainders, check that the remainder is smaller than the number we divide by, decide what the leftover means in a story (one more group, or leave it out), work backwards from groups and leftovers, and solve "what number am I?" riddles by making a list. Heuristics taught today: WORK BACKWARDS (start number = groups × size + leftover) and MAKE A LIST (list the numbers that fit one clue, then test each with the other clue). Materials: 25 counters per child (or beans or buttons), 6 small cups for groups, mini whiteboards and markers. Online: children use 25 small things at home (dried beans, buttons, LEGO bricks) and a few cups or bowls; children write on whiteboards. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 5 to 8 (two rounds) and three quick questions 8 to 11, explore 11 to 25.5 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25.5 to 36.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41.5, worksheet 41.5 to 72.5 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 69.5 everyone chooses), talk time 72.5 to 79.5 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 79.5 to 85, look back 85 to 88, stamp and close 88 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it. SPINE: Today's tool is Work backwards. Start from the answer and undo each step in reverse order, then check forwards. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p3l5-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Work backwards. Start from the answer and undo each step in reverse order, then check forwards. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l5-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 3 full bags, 1 left over. Listen for: 3 bags of 4 use 12 sweets. 1 sweet is left. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 6 sweets fill a bag, so 0 are left. Listen for: A leftover must be fewer than 6, otherwise another bag of 6 can be filled. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l5-warm1.note: Minutes 5 to 8. Leftover Lucky Dip. Play two rounds only (the first two cards, then the last two). Call each card in turn: "23 sweets, groups of 4." Children show the number of groups on one hand and the leftover on the other (fists for zero). Then click to reveal. Always ask for the times-table fact: "4 × 5 = 20, and 3 more makes 23." Answers: 23 in 4s = 5 groups, 3 left; 17 in 3s = 5 groups, 2 left; 26 in 8s = 3 groups, 2 left; 41 in 6s = 6 groups, 5 left. Extra calls if time: 30 in 7s (4 groups, 2 left), 50 in 9s (5 groups, 5 left). Watch for children who say "41 in 6s is 5 groups and 11 left": ask "Can 11 make another group of 6?"

p3l5-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 11. Write "r" for remainder. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. After each one ask: "How can we check?" (answer × divisor + remainder: 7 × 6 + 3 = 45). Answers: 1) 3 r 2 2) 4 r 2 3) 7 r 3. Three quick questions only; 50 ÷ 8 (6 r 2) and 63 ÷ 9 (7 r 0, nothing left over because 63 is in the 9 table) are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l5-explore1.note: Minutes 11 to 21. Predict first: "Which group size will leave nothing over?" Pairs make the groups with real counters (cups help) and fill in the table on a whiteboard. Results: 2s: 12 groups, 1 left. 3s: 8 groups, 1 left. 4s: 6 groups, 1 left. 5s: 5 groups, 0 left. 6s: 4 groups, 1 left. Hints: "Use a times-table fact: 6 × 4 = 24." Ready for more: "Try 49 counters. Which group sizes leave 1 over? Why?" (2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 all leave 1, because 48 is in all those tables; 7s leave 0.) Online: children use beans or buttons and use the whiteboard. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): 49 counters: which group sizes from 2 to 8 leave 1 over? Why? Answer: 49 = 48 + 1. Sizes 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 leave 1 over (48 is in all those tables). Size 5 leaves 4 and size 7 leaves 0 (49 = 7 x 7). Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l5-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 25.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather. Answers: 1) Groups of 5: 25 is in the 5 table. 2) 24 is in the 2, 3, 4 and 6 tables, and 25 is one more than 24. 3) No. If 4 were left over they would make another group. The leftover (remainder) is always smaller than the group size. This is the rule we use all lesson.

p3l5-teach1.note: Teach. Show 14 counters and make groups of 4 in front of the children. Click 1: the wrong picture (2 groups, 6 left). Ask: "What is wrong?" Click 2: the rule. Think-aloud: "When I divide, I keep making groups until I cannot make another one. So what is left must be smaller than the group size. Dividing by 4, the remainder can only be 0, 1, 2 or 3."

p3l5-we1.note: Click to reveal each step; ask the group to predict it first. Think-aloud: "38 sweets for 5 children. I count in 5s: 5 × 7 = 35, 5 × 8 = 40, too many. So each child gets 7. I used 35, so 3 are left. 3 is smaller than 5, good. I check: 7 × 5 + 3 = 38." Step 4 is new for most children: the next number in the 5 table is 40, so 2 more sweets would leave none over.

p3l5-try1.note: Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) 4 × 7 = 28, 1 left. b) 9 × 5 = 45, 7 left (7 is smaller than 9, so it is fine). c) 10 is bigger than 6, so another group fits: 6 × 6 = 36, 4 left. Ask: "How could Tom have noticed his mistake?"

p3l5-we2.note: Click through. Think-aloud: "50 people, vans of 8: 50 ÷ 8 = 6 r 2. Those 2 people cannot stay behind, so I need one more van: 7. But 50 cakes in boxes of 8 fill only 6 boxes; the 2 cakes do not make a full box. Same division, different answer. I read the question again." Ask: "Can you think of another story where we need one more group?" (tables, buses, boats, boxes to hold ALL the things).

p3l5-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 26 ÷ 4 = 6 r 2: the 2 children need a car, so 7. b) 40 ÷ 6 = 6 r 4: $4 is not enough for another toy, so 6. c) 45 ÷ 8 = 5 r 5: 5 whole pieces and 5 cm left over. Ask a child to explain a) and b) side by side.

p3l5-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Leaving a remainder that is as big as, or bigger than, the number we divide by (60 ÷ 7 = 7 r 11). (2) Giving the division answer when the story needs one more group (minibuses, boxes for ALL the eggs), or adding one when only full groups count (books she can buy). (3) Stopping at the first number that fits one clue in a riddle, without testing the other clue or finding ALL the numbers.

p3l5-break.note: Five minutes. 17 in 5s: 3 groups, 2 stomps. 23 in 4s: 5 groups, 3 stomps. 20 in 6s: 3 groups, 2 stomps. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l5-teachback.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 works backwards from bags and a leftover, then repacks). Heuristic: WORK BACKWARDS. Say: "Division splits the cookies into bags and a leftover. To go back, we put the bags together, groups × size, and add the leftover." Think-aloud: "9 bags of 6 is 54. Plus the 4 loose ones: 58. I check by dividing again: 58 ÷ 6 = 9 r 4. That matches the story." Ask: "Why must the leftover be less than 6?" (otherwise she could fill another bag).

p3l5-ws1.note: Minutes 43.5 to 55.5. Walk around. Ask "Is your remainder smaller than the number you divided by?" and "What happens to the leftover in this story?" before giving any help. For Q2c and Q2d check that pairs give two different answers. PAGE 1 CLOCK (43.5 to 55.5): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 8.5 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l5-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1: 6 × 7 = 42, 47 − 42 = 5; 48 is in the 6 table, so 1 more sticker. Q1c: 7 × 8 = 56, 60 − 56 = 4. Q2: 75 ÷ 9 = 8 r 3 (the 3 pupils need a bus: 9); 60 ÷ 7 = 8 r 4 ($4 is not enough: 8); 87 ÷ 6 = 14 r 3. Q3: 9 × 11 = 99, so 101 ÷ 9 = 11 r 2. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l5-teachlist.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Heuristic: MAKE A LIST. Think-aloud: "Two clues. I list the numbers for one clue, then test them with the other. The 5 clue gives a shorter list: 5 × 4 = 20, plus 4 is 24, then every 5 more: 29, 34, 39. Now test with 3." Stress: write the list in order so nothing is missed. If a question says "find ALL", do not stop at the first one. Check 29: 3 × 9 = 27, remainder 2 ✓; 5 × 5 = 25, remainder 4 ✓.

p3l5-teachbig.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Ask first: "Dividing by 6, could the remainder be 6? Could it be 7?" (No: another group would fit.) The biggest remainder is always one less than the number we divide by. Then click through.

p3l5-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Check that every child writes a list for Q4. Q6 (the party tables, if time) has no teaching slide: children who reach it fill the table until the rows match (4 standing, so the gap shrinks by 1 for each extra table). Keep Q3(b) and Q4(b) as (if time) exactly as printed.

p3l5-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4a: 43, 48, 53, 58; divided by 4 they leave 3, 0, 1, 2, so 53. Q4b (if time): remainder 5 when ÷ 6: 11, 17, 23, 29, 35, 41, 47; test ÷ 4: 11, 23, 35, 47 leave 3. Ask: "Why do they go up in 12s?" (12 is in both the 4 and 6 tables). Q5b: biggest remainder 7; 56 + 7 = 63. Q6: rows 11/7, 17/14, 23/21, 29/28, 35/35. With 8 at each table: 40 seats − 35 children = 5 empty. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l5-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) 43 (remainder 1 when ÷ 6: 43 and 49; 43 ÷ 4 = 10 r 3 ✓, 49 ÷ 4 = 12 r 1). 2) 9 r 7 (work backwards: 9 × 8 + 7 = 79; 79 ÷ 8 = 9 r 7). 3) 4 more (60 ÷ 8 = 7 r 4; the next box needs 64).

p3l5-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) Wednesday in 100 days (100 ÷ 7 = 14 r 2, so 2 days after Monday). Saturday 100 days ago (14 weeks back is Monday, then 2 more days back: Sunday, Saturday). 2) 7 pupils and 38 pens.

p3l5-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Q1: "Every 7 days we are back to Monday. So what matters is the leftover after the full weeks." Q2: "What changes between the two rows? How many more pens does each pupil get? Where do those extra pens come from?"

p3l5-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the remainder is what matters: full weeks bring us back to the same day. Many children count on 100 from Monday or say Tuesday; the table of days shows why it is 2 days on. For 100 days AGO, children often say Wednesday again: ask them to go backwards, so 2 days BEFORE Monday is Saturday. Q2: if children are stuck, act it out with 3 or 4 "pupils" and pens; a table (pupils 1, 2, 3 … with pens needed both ways) also works: 7 pupils is where 4 × 7 + 10 = 38 and 6 × 7 − 4 = 38 match.

p3l5-talk.note: Minutes 72.5 to 79.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Second question if time: "75 ÷ 9 = 8 r 3. Why was the minibus answer 9, not 8?" Answer: If the leftover were as big as the group size, we could make one more group, so the remainder is always smaller. The 3 pupils left over still need a seat, so we need one more minibus. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l5-exit.note: Minutes 79.5 to 85. Answer: 29 ÷ 4 = 7 r 1. 8 cars are needed: the 1 child left over still needs a car. Extension: Find the smallest number bigger than 1 that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 (61). Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l5-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 85 to 88. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Try. Ask the child to test one example, or a smaller case, before deciding. Say: "Pick one example and test it. What happens?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
